title: The Casino Trick Hiding in Your Phone
description: Why do casinos swap your cash for plastic? Case file #001 follows Larry (fictional) through one night in a casino: the chips, the 'house money' feeling, the arithmetic of two green pockets, the near miss that your brain counts as a win, a famous myth about casino clocks - and the same trick hiding in your phone.
sources: Raghubir, P. & Srivastava, J. (2008). Monopoly Money: The Effect of Payment Coupling and Form on Spending Behavior. Journal of Experimental Psychology: Applied, 14(3).
Thaler, R. H. & Johnson, E. J. (1990). Gambling with the House Money and Trying to Break Even: The Effects of Prior Outcomes on Risky Choice. Management Science, 36(6), 643-660.
Clark, L., Lawrence, A. J., Astley-Jones, F. & Gray, N. (2009). Gambling Near-Misses Enhance Motivation to Gamble and Recruit Win-Related Brain Circuitry. Neuron, 61(3).
Harrigan, K. A. (2007). Slot machine structural characteristics: Distorted player views of payback percentages. Journal of Gambling Issues, 20.
Friedman, B. (2000). Designing Casinos to Dominate the Competition. Institute for the Study of Gambling and Commercial Gaming, University of Nevada, Reno.
Mental Floss: Why Don't Casinos Have Windows? (Friedman on the clock myth).
Roulette maths: American wheel 2/38 = 5.26% house edge; European wheel 1/37 = 2.70%.
Larry is a fictional character. Archive-style scenes marked 'Reconstruction' are illustrations, not historical footage.

doc.headline: Gambling with the house money
doc.body: In experiments with real money, people who had just won became more willing to take risks, as if the winnings were not really their own. After a loss, bets that offered a chance to break even became especially attractive.

beats.text: After a win, people took bigger risks, as if the winnings weren't really theirs. They called it the house money effect.

beats.text: Here's the catch. The moment the dealer pushed those chips across the table, they stopped being the casino's money.

beats.text: They were Larry's. All along.
Eleven p.m.
The hundred is gone. So is a chunk of the five hundred.

beats.text: The house doesn't need luck, Larry. It has arithmetic.
Las Vegas, 1940. The wheel hasn't changed since. Neither has the arithmetic.

beats.say: Las Vegas, nineteen forty. The wheel hasn't changed since. Neither has the arithmetic.

beats.text: So let's do the arithmetic. An American roulette wheel has thirty-eight pockets. Thirty-six are red or black.
And two are green. Zero, and double zero.
Those two green pockets are the entire business model.
On almost every bet on the table, they give the house an edge of about five point two six percent.
In plain money: for every hundred dollars Larry bets, he can expect to lose about five dollars twenty-six.

visual.prompt: a plain unlettered green banknote with one corner neatly torn away, the torn corner floating just beside it, lying on green casino felt

beats.text: Bet a hundred dollars a hundred times, and the expected bill is five hundred and twenty-six dollars.

beats.text: Which, you'll notice, is more than Larry walked in with.

visual.prompt: {larry} turning out his empty trouser pockets with a sheepish grin

beats.text: Even a European wheel, with a single green zero, keeps about two point seven percent. The house always takes a slice.
Now Larry is behind, and he wants it back.

visual.prompt: {larry} rolling up his sleeves at the roulette table with grim determination

beats.text: Thaler and Johnson spotted this too: after a loss, any bet that offers a chance to break even suddenly looks very attractive.

beats.text: Here's the strange part. A near miss isn't a near win. It's a loss. A completely ordinary loss.

doc.headline: Gambling near-misses enhance motivation to gamble
doc.body: Volunteers played a simple slot machine in a brain scanner. Near-misses were rated as unpleasant, yet they increased the desire to keep playing and activated brain regions that also respond to wins.

beats.text: The near misses felt unpleasant. And yet they made people want to keep playing, and lit up the same brain circuits that respond to wins.

doc.headline: Slot machine structural characteristics
doc.body: The machine's 22 physical reel stops were mapped onto a hidden 64-stop virtual reel. On reel one, the top symbol landed just above the payline 8 times in 64, but on the payline only 2 times in 64.

beats.text: The reels you see are not the reels that count. Behind them sits a hidden virtual reel.

beats.text: Two a.m. And now, the famous part.
You've heard it. Casinos have no clocks and no windows, so you lose track of time.

beats.text: The story comes from the boom years of the Las Vegas Strip, and it's repeated in almost every video about casinos.

visual.credit: Home movie 010112_001 (1950s Las Vegas), Prelinger Archives / Internet Archive (public domain)

beats.text: There's just one problem.

visual.prompt: an enormous thick hardback book with a plain blank cloth cover lying on a wooden desk beside rolled-up architectural blueprints

beats.text: Bill Friedman, a former Las Vegas casino manager who wrote a six-hundred-page book on casino design, called the clock story a myth.

visual.prompt: a round wall clock on a plain casino wall

beats.text: By his account, it was the serious gamblers who wanted the clocks gone.

visual.prompt: an annoyed card player in a grey 1950s suit and hat glaring up at a round wall clock

beats.text: Friedman's real advice is more interesting. Don't build one big open hall. Build a maze.

visual.prompt: a 1950s architect at a drafting table drawing a winding maze on a large blueprint

beats.text: Low ceilings. Winding paths. Little nooks packed with machines, so the way out tends to wind past one more game.
No conspiracy about clocks. Just a floor plan where leaving takes a little more effort than staying.

visual.prompt: a tiny glowing exit sign far away at the end of a long winding corridor of slot machines

beats.text: Now, in fairness to the accused.
Chips aren't only a mind game. They're quick to count, easy to stack and weigh,

beats.text: So, the verdict.
And the defence, for next time.
Before you tap, before you buy the gems, before you swap money for anything shiny, ask one question: how many real dollars is this?
Because the house doesn't need you to lose. It just needs you to stop counting.

beats.text: No clocks in casinos? That's a myth.
Bill Friedman, who wrote a six-hundred-page book on casino design, called it exactly that.
By his account, serious gamblers wanted the clocks gone.
His real trick? A maze. Winding paths and machines in every nook.
So the next time someone tells you there are no clocks in casinos…
